questions.stem: A 24 year old man has had a cough for 7 weeks, with evening fevers, drenching night sweats and 5 kg weight loss. His uncle, who lives with the family, started treatment for 'a chest infection that needs six months of tablets' two months ago. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. He is thin, with crackles at the left apex and a small left supraclavicular node.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A chronic cough over 3 weeks with fever, night sweats, weight loss and apical crackles in a household contact of someone on 6 months of treatment is pulmonary TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Chronic cough, sweats, weight loss and a close contact = TB.

elim: An acute illness over days, not 7 weeks of sweats and weight loss.
Can cause sweats and nodes, but not a cough with apical crackles after household TB exposure.
Unlikely at 24 and does not explain the household contact.
Usually bilateral hilar nodes with few systemic symptoms; no infectious contact history.

steps.x: D: Pulmonary tuberculosis. Close contact with active TB is a key risk factor.

questions.stem: A 31 year old teacher is screened because a colleague in her staff room has smear-positive pulmonary TB. She feels completely well, with no cough, fever, sweats or weight loss. She had BCG at school. Examination is normal. Her interferon-gamma release assay is positive and her chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A positive screening test with no symptoms and a normal chest X-ray is latent TB: asymptomatic and non-infectious. IGRA is preferred because BCG does not cause false positives.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Positive IGRA + no symptoms + normal CXR = latent TB.

elim: She has no symptoms and a normal chest X-ray.
IGRA is not affected by previous BCG, which is why it is preferred here.
A severely unwell patient with innumerable tiny nodules on the X-ray.
Usually causes lung disease in people with structural lung damage; does not explain a positive IGRA after TB contact.

steps.x: C: Latent tuberculosis. Latent TB: positive test, no active disease, not infectious.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man who grew up in rural India has had a slowly enlarging patch on his left cheek for 2 years. It began as small reddish-brown papules that merged into a scaly red plaque with some scarring at the centre. When a glass slide is pressed on it, the papules look like apple jelly. He is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lupus vulgaris is the commonest form of cutaneous TB, typically in younger adult men: small discoloured papules or nodules that enlarge into scaly red plaques, with apple-jelly nodules on diascopy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A slowly spreading facial plaque with apple-jelly nodules = lupus vulgaris.

elim: A pearly nodule with telangiectasia in an older, sun-exposed person.
Scarring plaques with follicular plugging, without apple-jelly nodules on diascopy.
Silvery plaques on extensor surfaces, not a single facial plaque with apple-jelly papules.
Violaceous swelling of the nose and cheeks, usually in women with systemic sarcoid.

steps.x: C: Lupus vulgaris. Lupus vulgaris: the commonest cutaneous TB.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman who came from Somalia 2 years ago has a 3 month history of painless swelling on the right side of her neck, with evening fevers and 4 kg weight loss. There is a matted, non-tender mass of nodes with a small discharging sinus. Her chest is clear. Excision biopsy shows granulomas with central caseating necrosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: TB can affect almost any organ; lymph node TB gives matted nodes that may discharge through a sinus. Caseating granulomas are the hallmark of TB.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Matted nodes, sinus and caseating granulomas = TB lymphadenitis.

elim: Tender regional nodes after a cat scratch, with stellate microabscesses rather than caseation.
Rubbery nodes with Reed-Sternberg cells, not caseating granulomas.
Small tender nodes after an infection that resolve, not a matted mass with a sinus.
Non-caseating granulomas.

steps.x: E: Tuberculous lymphadenitis. Caseation separates TB from sarcoid (non-caseating).

questions.stem: A 74 year old man taking prednisolone 20 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica has had 4 weeks of fevers, sweats, poor appetite and 6 kg weight loss. He is now breathless. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. His liver is just palpable. A chest X-ray shows countless tiny nodules, each 1 to 2 mm, evenly scattered through both lungs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Countless 1 to 2 mm nodules ('millet seeds') with fever and wasting in an immunosuppressed man is miliary TB: haematogenous spread seeding many organs (here the liver). It is fatal if untreated.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: countless tiny nodules, each 1 to 2 mm
steps.x: Millet-seed nodules everywhere + fever + immunosuppression = miliary TB.

elim: Larger nodules of varying size; the fevers and sweats point to infection.
Bilateral ground-glass change, not innumerable millet-seed nodules.
Bat-wing shadowing with cardiomegaly and effusions.
Bilateral hilar nodes; not a febrile, wasting illness in an immunosuppressed man.

steps.x: B: Miliary tuberculosis. Miliary TB is haematogenous dissemination.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has 6 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss. Her chest X-ray shows right upper zone cavitation. Her rheumatologist started a new treatment 3 months ago because her joints were not controlled. She also takes folic acid, hydroxychloroquine, omeprazole and sulfasalazine.
questions.q: Which medication most likely increased her risk of this infection?
questions.e: Anti-TNF drugs such as infliximab are the classic immunosuppressive therapy that reactivates TB, because TNF-alpha is needed to keep granulomas intact. Patients are screened for latent TB before starting.

steps.x: The question asks: Which medication most likely increased her risk of this infection?

clues: started a new treatment 3 months ago
steps.x: New biologic for RA + TB = anti-TNF.

elim: A supplement with no effect on immunity.
Not significantly immunosuppressive and not linked with TB.
Does not impair granuloma formation.
Not linked with TB reactivation.

steps.x: C: Infliximab. Infliximab (anti-TNF) is a notable TB risk factor.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man from Pakistan has 5 months of thoracic back pain that wakes him at night, with sweats and weight loss. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. There is a tender kyphotic angulation at T10. Leg power and sensation are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on MRI of the spine?
o: Collapse of a single vertebra with a preserved disc and no soft tissue mass
Destruction of two adjacent vertebrae and the disc with a paravertebral abscess
L5/S1 disc prolapse compressing the nerve root
Multiple vertebral lesions sparing the discs
questions.e: Spinal TB (Pott's disease) spreads haematogenously to the vertebral body and crosses the disc, destroying adjacent vertebrae and forming a cold paravertebral (psoas) abscess, causing the gibbus.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on MRI of the spine?
Back pain, gibbus and systemic symptoms in someone from an endemic area = Pott's disease.

elim: Typical of osteoporotic fracture or myeloma.
Causes sciatica, not a thoracic gibbus with sweats.
Suggests metastases.
Ankylosing spondylitis, with morning stiffness.

steps.x: B: Destruction of two adjacent vertebrae and the disc with a paravertebral abscess. Pott's: two vertebrae, the disc between, and a cold abscess.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman whose partner is being treated for pulmonary TB has had 3 weeks of headache, low-grade fever and increasing confusion. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. She is drowsy with neck stiffness and a left sixth nerve palsy. CT head shows mild hydrocephalus. A lumbar puncture is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding in the cerebrospinal fluid?
o: Lymphocytes, high protein and very low glucose
Lymphocytes, normal protein and normal glucose
Neutrophils, high protein and low glucose
Oligoclonal bands with normal cell count
questions.e: TB meningitis is subacute, with cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus. CSF shows a lymphocytosis, very high protein and very low glucose.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding in the cerebrospinal fluid?

clues: partner is being treated for pulmonary TB
steps.x: Subacute meningitis, cranial nerve palsy and a TB contact = TB meningitis.

elim: Typical of viral meningitis.
Acute bacterial meningitis, with a much shorter history.
Subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Multiple sclerosis.

steps.x: A: Lymphocytes, high protein and very low glucose. TB meningitis CSF: lymphocytes, high protein, very low glucose.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man who moved from Eritrea a year ago has 2 months of productive cough, night sweats and loss of appetite. His trousers no longer fit. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 94 bpm, BP 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His sputum is positive for acid-fast bacilli.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Bilateral fine end-inspiratory crackles with clubbing
Cachexia, apical crackles and cervical lymphadenopathy
Dullness to percussion at both bases with raised JVP
Hyper-resonance with absent breath sounds on one side
questions.e: Pulmonary TB causes wasting (cachexia), crackles over the affected (usually upper) zone and lymphadenopathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
AFB-positive chronic cough with weight loss: expect cachexia, crackles and nodes.

elim: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
Asthma or COPD.
Bilateral effusions from heart failure.
Pneumothorax.

steps.x: C: Cachexia, apical crackles and cervical lymphadenopathy. TB exam: cachexia, crackles, lymphadenopathy.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man with HIV, who stopped his antiretrovirals a year ago, has 6 weeks of cough with occasional blood, fevers and night sweats. His CD4 count is 340 cells/µL. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. His chest X-ray shows left upper zone consolidation with a cavity (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Left upper zone consolidation with cavitation.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: HIV is a major TB risk factor at any CD4 count. Chronic cough, haemoptysis, sweats and an upper zone cavity is pulmonary TB; PCP needs a lower CD4 and looks different.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: 6 weeks of cough with occasional blood
left upper zone consolidation with a cavity
steps.x: HIV + chronic cough + upper zone cavity = TB.

elim: Purple skin lesions with nodular lung shadowing at low CD4 counts.
A swinging fever with foul sputum after aspiration, usually in a dependent segment.
Dry cough and desaturation on exertion with bilateral ground-glass change, usually CD4 <200.
Acute, lobar and without 6 weeks of sweats or cavitation.

steps.x: D: Pulmonary tuberculosis. HIV is a key TB risk factor.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl is screened because her grandfather, who lives with the family, has smear-positive pulmonary TB. She has had a mild cough and has been off her food for 3 weeks. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Her chest X-ray shows enlarged right hilar lymph nodes with a small right mid-zone opacity.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right hilar lymphadenopathy with a small parenchymal focus: primary TB.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: In a child with a recent household contact, a peripheral (Ghon) focus with hilar lymphadenopathy is primary TB: the first infection progressing to active disease rather than being contained as latent TB.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: grandfather, who lives with the family
steps.x: Child + recent contact + hilar nodes = primary TB.

elim: An infant viral illness with wheeze and crackles.
She has symptoms and an abnormal chest X-ray.
Possible cause of hilar nodes but the household TB contact explains it.
Seen in adults years after infection, typically with upper zone cavitation.

steps.x: E: Primary tuberculosis. Primary infection is either contained (latent) or progresses (primary active).

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with pulmonary TB and newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 count 45 cells/µL) started RIPE therapy 3 weeks ago and antiretroviral therapy 10 days ago. She had been improving but now has a high fever, worsening cough and enlarging, tender neck nodes. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Sputum cultures show fully sensitive organisms.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A paradoxical flare soon after starting ART, as the recovering immune system reacts to TB antigens, is IRIS. Delaying ART until about 4 weeks after starting TB treatment reduces the risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
A flare just after ART starts, with sensitive TB = IRIS.

elim: Causes jaundice and raised ALT, not enlarging nodes and fever.
Her organism is fully sensitive and she was improving.
Would cause failure to improve, not an inflammatory flare after ART.
Does not cause enlarging tender nodes.

steps.x: C: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Start ART about 4 weeks after TB treatment to reduce IRIS.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man started RIPE therapy for pulmonary TB 4 weeks ago. Overnight he developed an exquisitely painful, hot, swollen right big toe. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 134/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Investigations: serum urate 0.62 mmol/L (0.2–0.43). Aspirated joint fluid shows needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals.
questions.q: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Pyrazinamide reduces renal urate excretion, causing hyperuricaemia and gout, as well as arthralgia and hepatotoxicity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which drug is the most likely cause?

clues: painful, hot, swollen right big toe
steps.x: Gout on TB treatment = pyrazinamide.

elim: Causes optic neuritis, not gout.
Causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis.
Vitamin B6 given to prevent neuropathy; no effect on urate.
Causes hepatitis and orange secretions.

steps.x: C: Pyrazinamide. Pyrazinamide: gout, arthralgia, hepatotoxicity.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with alcohol dependence started treatment for pulmonary TB 2 months ago at another hospital. He now has burning pain and pins and needles in both feet, spreading up to his ankles. His prescription chart shows four TB drugs and no other tablets. Vibration sense is reduced to the knees.
questions.q: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy by depleting pyridoxine, especially in alcohol dependence and malnutrition. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) should have been given with it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which drug is the most likely cause?

clues: burning pain and pins and needles in both feet
steps.x: Neuropathy on RIPE, no B6 = isoniazid.

elim: Causes visual loss, not a glove-and-stocking neuropathy.
Causes gout and hepatotoxicity.
Causes uveitis and hepatitis; he is on rifampicin.
Causes hepatitis and orange secretions.

steps.x: B: Isoniazid. Always give pyridoxine with isoniazid.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman started treatment for pulmonary TB 5 days ago. She comes back worried because her urine is bright orange and her soft contact lenses have turned orange. She feels well. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm, BP 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Her liver tests are normal.
questions.q: Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Rifampicin turns urine, tears and sweat red or orange and stains soft contact lenses. It is harmless but she should be warned; rifampicin is also hepatotoxic and induces liver enzymes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which drug is the most likely cause?
Orange secretions = rifampicin.

elim: Causes visual disturbance, not discoloured secretions.
Causes peripheral neuropathy.
Causes gout and hepatotoxicity.
Vitamin B6 does not colour secretions.

steps.x: E: Rifampicin. Rifampicin: orange secretions, hepatotoxicity, enzyme induction.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy has had a cough, poor feeding and weight loss for 6 weeks. His father has just been diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary TB. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 120 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His chest X-ray shows right hilar lymphadenopathy. He cannot produce sputum.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to obtain a sample for mycobacterial culture?
questions.e: Young children swallow their sputum, so early-morning gastric aspirates are sent for AFB smear and culture when sputum cannot be produced.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to obtain a sample for mycobacterial culture?
No sputum in a young child = gastric aspirate.

elim: Mycobacteria are not reliably grown from routine blood cultures.
No features of meningitis.
Does not sample the lower airway.
For renal TB, not pulmonary disease.

steps.x: B: Early-morning gastric aspirates. Children: gastric aspirate; adults: bronchoalveolar lavage.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman from Bangladesh has 2 months of dry cough, sweats and weight loss. Her chest X-ray shows right upper zone fibronodular shadowing. Despite nebulised hypertonic saline she cannot produce any sputum. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When an adult cannot produce sputum, even after induction, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage provides samples for smear, culture and PCR.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
No sputum in an adult with suspected TB = BAL.

elim: Too invasive as a first step; lavage samples the airway for culture.
Shows infection but cannot confirm active disease.
Shows exposure, not active disease.
For sarcoidosis.

steps.x: A: Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage. BAL when sputum cannot be obtained.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with bronchiectasis has 3 months of cough and weight loss. Sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli. His team know that other mycobacteria, such as Mycobacterium avium complex, also stain acid-fast and want to know within a day or two whether this is M. tuberculosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Nucleic acid amplification (PCR) of the sputum
questions.e: The AFB smear is not specific because all mycobacteria are acid-fast. PCR on respiratory samples gives a rapid, specific diagnosis of M. tuberculosis (and rifampicin resistance) while culture grows.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
Smear positive but species uncertain, need speed = PCR.

elim: Cannot identify the species.
Shows immune memory of TB infection, not the identity of the organism in the sputum.
Shows exposure, not the organism.
All mycobacteria stain positive, so it cannot distinguish them.

steps.x: D: Nucleic acid amplification (PCR) of the sputum. PCR supports rapid diagnosis; the smear is not specific.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man from Zimbabwe is diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary TB. He has no other medical history and says he has 'never been at risk' of sexually transmitted infections. His baseline U&Es, LFTs and full blood count are sent before treatment, and he is keen to start tablets today.
questions.q: Which additional investigation should be offered to him?
questions.e: Everyone investigated for TB should be offered an HIV test, whatever their stated risk, because HIV changes TB management (ART timing, drug interactions).

steps.x: The question asks: Which additional investigation should be offered to him?
Every TB patient gets an HIV test.

elim: No features of connective tissue disease.
Used in sarcoidosis.
For cystic fibrosis.
Not routinely needed for TB.

steps.x: B: HIV test. Offer HIV testing to all patients with TB.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with newly confirmed pulmonary TB is about to start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. U&Es, LFTs and a full blood count have been taken. She wears glasses for reading and drives a bus for a living, so she is anxious about any effect on her sight.
questions.q: Which additional baseline assessment is most important before she starts treatment?
o: Visual acuity and colour vision testing
questions.e: Ethambutol can cause toxic optic neuropathy with reduced acuity and red-green colour blindness, so baseline visual acuity and colour vision (Ishihara) are checked alongside U&Es, LFTs and FBC.

steps.x: The question asks: Which additional baseline assessment is most important before she starts treatment?
Ethambutol = eyes: test vision first.

elim: Needed for aminoglycosides such as streptomycin, not RIPE.
No cardiotoxicity from RIPE.
Neuropathy is prevented with pyridoxine; baseline studies are not routine.
Not needed before TB treatment.

steps.x: E: Visual acuity and colour vision testing. Baseline vision testing before ethambutol.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man from the UK, who never had BCG, lives with his brother who has smear-positive pulmonary TB. He is well. A Mantoux test is read at 72 hours and shows 8 mm of induration. His chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of the Mantoux test?
o: Uninterpretable as it was read at 72 hours
questions.e: A Mantoux induration of 5 mm or more is positive. With no symptoms and a normal chest X-ray, he has latent TB infection.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of the Mantoux test?
Mantoux 5 mm or more = positive.

elim: 8 mm is above the 5 mm threshold.
An induration of 5 mm or more is positive.
He never had BCG.
48 to 72 hours is the correct reading time.

steps.x: D: Positive: evidence of TB infection. Mantoux positive at 5 mm or more.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman from the Philippines has had a productive cough for 3 months with haemoptysis, evening fevers and 7 kg weight loss. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. There are crackles below the right clavicle.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Right upper zone shadowing with a cavity.

questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
o: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lungs
Dense left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms
Large right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift
Right upper zone fibronodular shadowing with cavitation
questions.e: Post-primary TB causes patchy or fibronodular opacification mainly in the upper zones, where high oxygen tension favours the aerobic organism, and caseation produces cavities.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
TB loves the apices: upper zone shadowing and cavities.

elim: Typical of sarcoidosis.
Pulmonary fibrosis.
Lobar pneumonia.
Possible in TB but does not fit apical crackles.

steps.x: E: Right upper zone fibronodular shadowing with cavitation. CXR in TB: upper zone opacification and cavitation.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man from Romania has 2 months of productive cough and night sweats. Three early-morning sputum samples are sent. The respiratory consultant wants the quickest possible microscopy result to decide whether he is smear-positive and needs isolation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate method of examining the sputum?
questions.e: Sputum is examined for acid-fast bacilli with Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine stain. Auramine fluorescence microscopy is the fastest because slides can be scanned at lower power.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate method of examining the sputum?
Fastest AFB smear = auramine.

elim: Mycobacteria stain poorly with Gram stain.
For Cryptococcus.
The gold standard but takes weeks.
For Pneumocystis.

steps.x: A: Auramine-rhodamine fluorescence microscopy. AFB smear: Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine (fastest).

questions.stem: A 52 year old man who moved from Lithuania has smear-positive pulmonary TB. He took an incomplete course of TB treatment 5 years ago, so the team is concerned about drug resistance and needs a full sensitivity profile for all first-line drugs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide his long-term treatment?
o: Mycobacterial culture with drug sensitivity testing
questions.e: Mycobacterial culture is the gold standard: the most sensitive test and the one that provides full drug sensitivities, though it takes weeks because the organism grows slowly. PCR can flag rifampicin resistance early.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide his long-term treatment?
Sensitivities to every drug need the organism grown.

elim: Shows the extent of disease, not drug sensitivities.
Only shows TB infection.
Only shows exposure.
Shows bacilli but not their sensitivities.

steps.x: D: Mycobacterial culture with drug sensitivity testing. Culture: gold standard, slow, gives sensitivities.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman who works in a nursery is admitted with 2 months of cough, sweats and weight loss and right upper zone cavitation on chest X-ray. Sputum has been sent for AFB smear, PCR and culture. The registrar says he will contact public health 'once culture confirms TB'.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Ask the nursery to inform public health
Notification is not needed if she is treated
Notify only if the PCR is positive
Notify public health now on clinical suspicion
questions.e: TB is notifiable: public health is notified on suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation, so contact tracing can begin. Her nursery contacts make this urgent.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?
Suspected TB = notify now.

elim: The doctor is responsible.
TB is notifiable.
Notification does not wait for lab results.
Culture takes weeks; contacts (including nursery children) would be left at risk.

steps.x: D: Notify public health now on clinical suspicion. Notify on suspicion; never wait for culture.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man from Somalia has biopsy-proven tuberculous lymphadenitis of the neck. He has no neurological symptoms and his chest X-ray is clear. PCR shows no rifampicin resistance. His HIV test is negative and his baseline liver tests are normal. He weighs 64 kg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Surgical excision of the nodes alone
questions.e: Active TB without CNS involvement, including lymph node TB, starts with quadruple RIPE therapy for 2 months, followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
Active TB, no CNS = RIPE intensive phase.

elim: A regimen for Mycobacterium avium complex.
Monotherapy is for latent TB only.
A latent TB regimen.
Drug treatment is still required.

steps.x: D: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. RIPE for 2 months first.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman with fully sensitive pulmonary TB has completed 2 months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and pyridoxine. Her cough has settled and she has gained weight. She has no CNS involvement, and her liver tests and visual acuity have stayed normal throughout.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for the next 4 months?
questions.e: After 2 months of RIPE, the continuation phase is rifampicin and isoniazid (with pyridoxine) for a further 4 months, a total of 6 months.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment for the next 4 months?
2 months RIPE, then 4 months RI.

elim: These are stopped after the intensive phase.
Monotherapy risks resistance in active disease.
Stopping at 2 months risks relapse; total treatment is 6 months.
All four drugs are only needed for the first 2 months.

steps.x: D: Rifampicin and isoniazid. Continuation phase: rifampicin + isoniazid for 4 months.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with HIV has newly diagnosed, fully sensitive pulmonary TB. His antiretroviral regimen contains a boosted protease inhibitor, which his HIV physician does not want to change because of previous resistance. Rifampicin would markedly lower its levels.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to the standard TB regimen?
o: Omit rifamycins and treat for 6 months
Stop antiretroviral therapy during TB treatment
questions.e: Rifabutin can substitute for rifampicin when drug interactions are a problem, as it is a much weaker enzyme inducer.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate change to the standard TB regimen?

clues: Rifampicin would markedly lower its levels
steps.x: Rifampicin interaction = swap to rifabutin.

elim: Does not solve the interaction.
A rifamycin-free regimen is less effective.
Rifabutin replaces rifampicin, not isoniazid.
Unsafe, and not needed.

steps.x: D: Replace rifampicin with rifabutin. Rifabutin substitutes for rifampicin.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man who had a kidney transplant 3 years ago takes tacrolimus. He is screened after his daughter is diagnosed with pulmonary TB. He is well, his IGRA is positive and his chest X-ray is normal. His transplant team want to avoid any drug that would reduce tacrolimus levels.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
o: No treatment, as latent TB is not infectious
questions.e: Latent TB is treated with 3 months of isoniazid and rifampicin, or 6 months of isoniazid alone (with pyridoxine) when rifamycins are contraindicated, for example after transplant.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment?

clues: IGRA is positive and his chest X-ray is normal
steps.x: Latent TB + rifamycins contraindicated = 6 months isoniazid.

elim: A live vaccine, contraindicated in immunosuppression, and he is already infected.
Latent TB in a transplant recipient carries a high reactivation risk.
Rifampicin would lower tacrolimus levels, risking rejection.
For active TB, which he does not have.

steps.x: B: Isoniazid with pyridoxine for 6 months. Latent TB: 3HR, or 6H if no rifamycins.

questions.stem: A 27 year old chef is found to have latent TB on contact screening and has started isoniazid and rifampicin with pyridoxine. She feels well, has no cough and her chest X-ray is normal. Her manager asks whether she must stay off work until treatment finishes.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: She may only work wearing an FFP3 mask
She must stay off work for 2 weeks
She must stay off work for 3 months
She should move to a role away from food
questions.e: People with latent TB are not infectious and cannot transmit the disease, so there is no restriction on employment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?
Latent = not infectious = no restriction.

elim: No transmission risk.
Applies to infectious pulmonary TB, not latent TB.
Latent TB is not infectious.
Latent TB is not spread by food or contact.

steps.x: A: She can work normally. No work restriction in latent TB.

questions.stem: A 22 year old student shares a flat with a man who has smear-positive pulmonary TB. She has never had BCG. She is well, her chest X-ray is normal and her Mantoux test shows 0 mm of induration. A repeat test 6 weeks later is again negative. She has no medical conditions.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Mantoux-negative, unvaccinated contacts of pulmonary or laryngeal TB under 35 are offered BCG.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?
Unvaccinated, Mantoux-negative contact under 35 = BCG.

elim: She has no evidence of infection to treat.
She is unprotected and has ongoing exposure risk.
For latent TB, which she does not have.
For active TB.

steps.x: A: BCG vaccination. BCG for Mantoux-negative contacts under 35.

questions.stem: A 42 year old staff nurse on a respiratory ward cared for a patient with smear-positive laryngeal TB before isolation. She has no record of BCG and no scar. She is well, her chest X-ray is normal and her Mantoux test is negative. Occupational health reviews her.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Exclude her from work for 6 weeks
No vaccination as she is over 35
questions.e: BCG is offered to unvaccinated, Mantoux-negative contacts under 35, and to those over 35 who are healthcare workers.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step?
Over 35 but a healthcare worker = still offer BCG.

elim: She is well and not infectious.
The age limit does not apply to healthcare workers.
She has no infection to treat.
She has no symptoms or sputum.

steps.x: A: BCG vaccination. BCG age limit is waived for healthcare workers.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man with HIV (CD4 count 150 cells/µL) lives with his cousin, who has smear-positive pulmonary TB. He has never had BCG. He is well, his chest X-ray is normal and his IGRA is negative. A nurse suggests giving BCG to protect him.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Do not give BCG, as it is a live vaccine
Give a double dose of BCG
Give BCG after a repeat negative IGRA
Give BCG once he starts antiretrovirals
questions.e: BCG is a live attenuated vaccine and is contraindicated in immunosuppressed patients, including HIV, because it can disseminate.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate response?
Immunosuppressed = no live vaccines.

elim: Never appropriate.
BCG remains contraindicated.
A live vaccine in a severely immunosuppressed patient risks disseminated BCG infection.
Still immunosuppressed; not used.

steps.x: A: Do not give BCG, as it is a live vaccine. BCG is contraindicated in immunosuppression.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man is 7 weeks into RIPE treatment for pulmonary TB. He has noticed blurred vision in both eyes and finds that red traffic lights look washed out. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 74 bpm, BP 132/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Visual acuity has fallen from 6/6 to 6/18 in both eyes since baseline.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue all drugs and review in 1 month
Stop ethambutol and refer urgently to ophthalmology
questions.e: Reduced acuity and red-green colour loss on RIPE is ethambutol toxic optic neuropathy: stop ethambutol at once and refer to ophthalmology.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: red traffic lights look washed out
steps.x: Colour vision loss on TB drugs = stop ethambutol.

elim: Prevents isoniazid neuropathy; does not treat optic neuropathy.
Continuing risks permanent visual loss.
Isoniazid optic atrophy is seen with parenteral use; ethambutol is the usual cause.
Causes orange secretions and hepatitis, not optic neuropathy.

steps.x: C: Stop ethambutol and refer urgently to ophthalmology. Ethambutol: toxic optic neuropathy.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman started RIPE for pulmonary TB 3 weeks ago. She now has nausea, vomiting and yellow eyes. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 88 bpm, BP 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Investigations: bilirubin 68 µmol/L (<21), ALT 410 U/L (<40), ALP 150 U/L (30–130). Her baseline liver tests were normal. Viral hepatitis serology is negative.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue all drugs and recheck in 2 weeks
Stop rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide and monitor liver tests
questions.e: Rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide are all hepatotoxic. With jaundice and a large ALT rise they are stopped and liver tests monitored, then drugs are reintroduced one at a time.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Drug-induced hepatitis on RIPE: stop the hepatotoxic three.

elim: Jaundice with ALT over 5 times normal requires stopping hepatotoxic drugs.
Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic.
Rifabutin is also hepatotoxic.
No duct obstruction; the pattern is hepatocellular.

steps.x: C: Stop rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide and monitor liver tests. Pyrazinamide and rifampicin (and isoniazid) are hepatotoxic.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man starts treatment for pulmonary TB. He is warned that one of his four drugs will turn his urine and tears orange and interacts with many other medicines by inducing liver enzymes. The pharmacist explains how this drug kills the bacteria.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of this drug?
questions.e: Rifampicin (orange secretions, enzyme induction) inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of action of this drug?
Orange urine = rifampicin = RNA polymerase.

elim: Ethambutol.
Fluoroquinolones.
Isoniazid.
Aminoglycosides such as streptomycin.

steps.x: C: Inhibition of bacterial RNA polymerase. Rifampicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman on treatment for pulmonary TB develops reduced colour vision and is told one drug will be stopped. She asks how that drug worked against the bacteria, as she was told it attacks the cell wall in a different way from isoniazid.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of the drug being stopped?
o: Activity in the acidic environment of macrophages
questions.e: Ethambutol, which causes optic neuropathy, inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall. Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the mechanism of action of the drug being stopped?
Colour vision loss = ethambutol = arabinogalactan.

elim: Pyrazinamide.
Rifampicin.
Isoniazid, which also targets the cell wall.
Beta-lactams; mycobacteria are intrinsically resistant.

steps.x: B: Inhibition of arabinogalactan synthesis. Ethambutol inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis.

questions.stem: A pharmacology tutor explains that one first-line TB drug is particularly good at killing the semi-dormant bacilli that survive inside macrophages and in inflamed caseous tissue, which is why it shortens treatment to 6 months. It is also the drug that causes gout.
questions.q: Which property explains this drug's activity?
o: It is active in an acidic environment
It is concentrated in the urine
questions.e: Pyrazinamide is active in the acidic intracellular environment of macrophages, killing bacilli that other drugs miss.

steps.x: The question asks: Which property explains this drug's activity?
Gout drug, intracellular killing = pyrazinamide, acid-active.

elim: Ethambutol.
Rifampicin.
Isoniazid.
Not the basis of its sterilising action.

steps.x: D: It is active in an acidic environment. Pyrazinamide works in the acidic macrophage environment.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy from a 30 year old woman with TB shows clusters of epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells around a centre of caseous necrosis, with a cuff of lymphocytes. Ziehl-Neelsen staining shows red rods, and the culture is expected to take several weeks.
questions.q: Which immune mechanism produces this histological appearance?
questions.e: M. tuberculosis is an acid-fast, slow-growing intracellular organism. It triggers a Th1 cell-mediated response (interferon-gamma activates macrophages), forming granulomas that wall off the organism.

steps.x: The question asks: Which immune mechanism produces this histological appearance?

clues: epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells
steps.x: Granuloma = Th1 cell-mediated immunity.

elim: Type II hypersensitivity; does not form granulomas.
Type I hypersensitivity.
Type III hypersensitivity.
Forms abscesses, not granulomas.

steps.x: E: Th1 cell-mediated macrophage activation. Th1 response causes granuloma formation.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman in a care home, who had TB as a child in Ireland, develops 2 months of cough, weight loss and right upper zone cavitation. She has had no recent contact with anyone with TB and has never been treated with immunosuppressive drugs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her illness?
o: Haematogenous spread from a bone focus
New infection from a care home visitor
Reactivation of dormant bacilli as immunity wanes with age
Type I hypersensitivity to mycobacterial antigens
questions.e: After primary infection, bacilli can lie dormant within granulomas (latent TB). Reactivation occurs years later when cell-mediated immunity wanes with immunosuppression, HIV or ageing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her illness?

clues: never been treated with immunosuppressive drugs
steps.x: Old infection + old age = reactivation.

elim: No evidence of extrapulmonary disease.
Does not explain the previous TB history.
No known contact; reactivation is far more likely.
Not the mechanism of TB.

steps.x: D: Reactivation of dormant bacilli as immunity wanes with age. Reactivation when immunity wanes.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 90 cells/µL has pulmonary TB. Two months later he develops thoracic back pain, and MRI shows destruction of T8 and T9 with a paravertebral abscess. The infection has reached a site distant from the lungs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of spread to the spine?
questions.e: Extrapulmonary TB (bone, lymph nodes, meninges, GI tract) arises from lymphatic and haematogenous dissemination, and is more common in immunocompromised hosts such as people with advanced HIV.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely route of spread to the spine?
Distant organ TB = blood-borne spread, commoner in the immunocompromised.

elim: TB of the spine arises from blood-borne seeding of the vertebral body.
Causes GI TB, not spinal TB.
Causes cutaneous TB.
Not a route for TB.

steps.x: B: Haematogenous dissemination. Extrapulmonary spread is lymphatic/haematogenous.
